title: The Thousand Torii
subtitle: Beneath Ten Thousand Vermilion Gates, the Foxes Are Counting Their Tails

setting.name: Heian-kyō, the Capital of Peace, and the Shrine of a Thousand Torii
setting.description: Heian-kyō (the mythic analog of real Kyoto ⛩️) is the ancient imperial capital, a city of willow-lined canals, lantern-warmed teahouses, and ten thousand shrines tucked between cedar hills. Pilgrims throng its grid of narrow lanes by day; by night the geisha district glows like a string of paper coals, and the temple bells count the hours across the rooftops. Above it all, climbing the eastern mountain in an unbroken tunnel of vermilion gates, stands the Great Shrine of a Thousand Torii — sacred to Inari Ōkami, the rice-god, whose white-fox messengers (kitsune 🦊) carry prayers between the worlds. The party arrives carrying a fox-sealed offering and finds the kami restless: lanterns gutter without wind, fortunes come up blank, and beneath the mountain of gates a conspiracy of foxes is counting toward nine tails.
setting.atmosphere: Refined, ritual-bound, and quietly uncanny. Incense and cedar smoke hang in the cold mountain air; the clack of geta sandals echoes off lacquered walls. Beauty everywhere, and obligation behind it — every bow has a meaning, every fox a possible god in disguise. By the thousand torii, daylight glows blood-warm through the painted gates while shadows pool blue-black between them. After dusk, fox-fire onibi 🏮 drift the cedar slopes, and something with too many tails laughs just out of sight. The line between a blessing and a curse is one mispronounced syllable wide.

keyLocations.name: The Willow Canal District (Yanagi-bashi)
keyLocations.description: The party's gateway into Heian-kyō: a quarter of stone-banked canals where weeping willows trail their fingers in slow green water and flat-bottomed boats pole between machiya townhouses with latticed wooden fronts. Merchants hawk grilled rice-cakes and sweet bean buns from awning-shaded stalls, monks beg with iron bowls, and the air smells of river-mud, charcoal, and frying tofu. It is the city's reception hall — and its rumor mill.
features: A humpbacked stone bridge where a blind biwa-player recites the news of the city for coppers
A roadside Jizō statue wrapped in a red bib, where travelers leave a pebble for safe passage (✅ Real custom: stacking stones / offering bibs to Jizō, guardian of travelers and children)
The Sō-ke Exchange House, a money-changer and post-station where the party's letter of introduction can be verified
A noodle stall, the Slurping Crane, whose owner Old Kenji hears everything spoken over a hot bowl
encounters: Roleplaying with the blind biwa-player, who 'sees' more than sighted folk and warns that 'the gates have begun to argue among themselves'
A tanuki in merchant's guise tries to pay for goods with leaves glamoured to look like gold (✅ Real folklore: tanuki leaf-money); catching him earns a grudging favor
Pickpocket children working the bridge crowd — a soft introduction to the city's underbelly and to the rival shinobi watching from a rooftop
secrets: The pickpocket children are unwitting lookouts for a malicious kitsune cell operating from beneath the shrine; one child carries a fox-fur charm she 'found' that is actually a tracking talisman
Old Kenji of the Slurping Crane is a retired shrine-warden who knows the proper sequence to enter the inner shrine safely — if the party treats him with courtesy and orders a bowl correctly

keyLocations.name: The Lantern Teahouse District (Hanagiku-machi)
keyLocations.description: The fantasy analog of real Gion 🏮 — a hushed warren of wooden teahouses (ochaya) and lantern-lit lanes where geisha (here called geiko) and their apprentices (maiko) move like drifting petals between engagements. Red paper lanterns hang in rows beneath deep eaves; the pluck of a shamisen and a woman's low laughter spill from upper rooms. It is the most refined quarter of the capital and the most dangerous to one's reputation — and, this season, to one's life.
features: The Hundred-Petal Teahouse, the district's finest, where introductions and secrets are traded over flawless tea
Narrow stone lanes lit entirely by red lanterns; voices carry, so intrigue is conducted in elegant indirection
A small Inari sub-shrine at the lane's end with a pair of stone fox-statues, each holding a key, a sheaf of rice, a jewel, or a scroll in its mouth
encounters: A formal tea engagement with the geiko Yumesaki, who carries the other half of the party's fox-sealed offering and a warning
A benevolent kitsune in maiko disguise tests the party's manners; rudeness loses her aid, courtesy gains a powerful ally
A masked figure flees across the rooftops when the party arrives — the rival shinobi, gathering intelligence on the offering
secrets: Yumesaki is herself a hundred-year fox who has chosen to protect the capital; she is the party's truest ally but cannot reveal her nature without being driven out
The stone fox holding a SCROLL in its mouth points (its gaze) toward the hidden entrance to the foxes' undershrine; the one holding a KEY conceals a real iron key in a hollow behind it

keyLocations.name: The Thousand Torii Path (Senbon-Torii)
keyLocations.description: The shrine's beating heart: a path that climbs the eastern mountain through a tunnel of perhaps ten thousand vermilion torii gates ⛩️ set so close their crossbeams nearly touch, each donated and inscribed on its back with a merchant's name and prayer (inspired by real Fushimi Inari-taisha). Sunlight strains red-orange through the lacquer; the temperature drops as you climb into old cedar forest. Stone fox-statues (kitsune) flank the way, moss-furred and watchful, white bibs at their throats. Where the path forks, the gates seem to whisper, and the deeper you go, the fewer pilgrims you meet.
features: Ten thousand vermilion torii in a near-continuous tunnel; the gates are donated by merchants and inscribed on the reverse (✅ Real: at Fushimi Inari, businesses donate the gates and their names appear on the back)
Branching forks where the tunnel splits and rejoins, easy to lose one's bearings without a clear head
Moss-covered stone fox-statues at every landing, some wearing red bibs, some with offerings of fried tofu (abura-age) at their feet (✅ Real: fried tofu is the traditional offering to Inari's foxes)
A halfway clearing with a tiny tea-rest and a rack of omikuji fortunes fluttering in the wind (✅ Real: tie a bad omikuji to a rack/pine to leave the bad luck behind)
encounters: Onibi (fox-fire will-o'-wisps 🔥) drift between the gates after dusk, luring pilgrims off the path into the ravine
A possessed kasa-obake (one-eyed, one-legged paper-umbrella yōkai) ambushes from among the votive umbrellas left at a landing
A 'lost pilgrim' who is actually a malicious one-tail kitsune scout, testing whether the party can tell friend from foe
secrets: Reading the names inscribed on the BACKS of the gates reveals that one merchant house — the Akagane (Copper) family — has donated a suspiciously huge run of new gates all at once, paid for in fox-gold; their gates conceal the descent to the undershrine
The omikuji at the halfway rest have ALL come up 'great curse' (dai-kyō) for a month — the kami's warning that something is wrong beneath the mountain

keyLocations.name: The Pillar Temple of the Pure Water (Kiyozuki-dera)
keyLocations.description: A great wooden Buddhist temple on the neighboring hillside (inspired by real Kiyomizu-dera 🛕), its broad worship hall thrust out over the steep slope on a forest of tall wooden pillars and crossbeams joined without a single nail. From its terrace, the whole capital spreads below in a haze of cooking-smoke and lantern light. A sacred spring splits into three channels at the cliff's foot, and pilgrims drink from one (and only one) with a long-handled ladle. Being a TEMPLE, not a shrine, its etiquette differs — and getting it wrong here has consequences.
features: A cantilevered terrace held aloft by a lattice of tall wooden pillars, dizzyingly high over the slope (✅ Real: Kiyomizu's stage is built on a pillar framework with no nails)

The three-channel sacred waterfall (the Otowa spring), each channel said to grant a different boon — but drinking from more than one is greedy and forfeits all (✅ Real: at Otowa-no-taki you choose ONE of three streams)
A great roofed temple gate and a vermilion pagoda — visibly different from the bare torii of a shrine (✅ Real: temples have roofed gates/pagodas; shrines have torii)
A hall of a thousand small Kannon statues, where a hidden monk-scholar keeps records of fox-sightings
encounters: Consulting the abbot Genmyō, who explains the kitsune politics: not all foxes are foes, and Inari's own messengers are at war with the nine-tail aspirants
A test of reverence: clapping (a shrine gesture) inside this Buddhist temple draws icy disapproval and, narratively, 'wakes something listening'
A novice monk, secretly charmed by a fox, who feeds the conspiracy information and must be gently freed
secrets: Abbot Genmyō holds the second half of the ritual the party needs: the words of sealing that bind a malicious fox without harming a benevolent one

Drinking from the temple's CENTER spring channel grants a one-time blessing (advantage on the first save vs. fox illusion in the finale) — but only to a character who took just one stream, honoring the custom

keyLocations.name: The Undershrine of Nine Tails (Kuzunoha-no-Miya)
keyLocations.description: Hidden beneath the thousand torii, reached through a gap behind the Akagane family's newest gates: a sunken Inari shrine drowned in cedar-root and fox-fire, its vermilion long faded to the color of old blood 💀. Hundreds of small stone foxes line the dark, their eyes catching the onibi glow. At its center sits a black-lacquered altar where a clever one-tail fox named Hōen schemes to devour the spirits of his elders and ascend to nine tails — the mark of a god. The truly old foxes of the shrine are not all complicit; some are prisoners, sealed in stone, waiting for someone clever and kind enough to tell them apart.
features: A drowned vermilion shrine lit only by drifting onibi fox-fire, ankle-deep in cold cedar litter and runoff
Rows of stone fox-statues, some of which are PETRIFIED living kitsune (benevolent elders trapped by Hōen) and some of which are merely stone
A black-lacquer altar bearing a censer of nine notches — one filled for each elder-spirit Hōen has consumed
The Tail-Counting Mirror, a bronze mirror that shows a fox's true number of tails to anyone who looks while speaking the truth
encounters: Hōen the one-tail schemer and his charmed thralls — the climactic confrontation, winnable by sealing rather than slaughter
Distinguishing trapped allies (stone foxes that weep real tears) from Hōen's stone decoys before the fight tips against the party
Freed elder foxes turning the tide if the party showed them mercy and read the situation correctly
secrets: Hōen has only ONE tail; his power is theft and illusion, not true strength — if his stolen spirits are released back to their stone bodies, he is left a frightened, ordinary fox
The Tail-Counting Mirror reflects the geiko Yumesaki (if present) as a NINE-tail — confirming she is an ancient guardian, not a foe, for any player still suspicious of her

synopsis: The party arrives in the imperial capital of Heian-kyō carrying a sacred offering sealed with a fox-paw print, charged with delivering it to the Great Shrine of a Thousand Torii. They quickly learn the kami are restless: fortunes come up cursed, lanterns gutter without wind, and pilgrims who climb the vermilion gates do not all come back down. Working the canal district, the lantern-lit teahouses, and the great pillar-temple across the valley, the party uncovers a conspiracy among the kitsune — Inari's fox-messengers. A clever, malicious one-tail fox named Hōen has been devouring his elders' spirits to ascend toward nine tails and the rank of a god, sealing the benevolent elders into stone to silence them. The party must master shrine etiquette and the city's intrigue, learn the words of sealing from a temple abbot, tell true foxes from false (with help from a hundred-year fox disguised as a geiko), and descend into the drowned undershrine to stop Hōen — not by simple slaughter, but by freeing the spirits he stole and exposing how few tails he truly has. Throughout, every shrine ritual, polite phrase, and bowl of noodles is drawn from the real Kyoto and clearly flagged for the players preparing for a journey to the land itself.
hook: At a roadside post-station beneath drifting cherry petals, a white fox with eyes like wet amber pads up to the party, drops a folded letter sealed with a paw-print of vermilion ink, and bows — actually bows — before vanishing. The letter, in an exquisite court hand, begs the bearer to carry the enclosed offering (a small lacquered box, warm to the touch and faintly humming) to the Great Shrine of a Thousand Torii in Heian-kyō, and to place it in the hands of 'one who knows how many tails the moon has.' It warns: the gates have begun to argue among themselves; trust the courteous fox and beware the clever one; and whatever happens, do not open the box until you stand before the altar. The capital is one day's walk along the torii road. 🦊⛩️

culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: 'Konnichiwa' (kon-nee-chee-WAH) = hello/good day. 'Sumimasen' (soo-mee-mah-SEN) = excuse me / sorry / to flag a server — the single most useful word in Japan. 'Arigatō gozaimasu' (ah-ree-gah-TOH go-zai-mahss) = thank you very much. A small bow from the waist accompanies most of these; the deeper and slower the bow, the more respect or apology it conveys. You don't need to bow back to a shop clerk's bow — a nod is fine.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: In Hinomoto a bow held a beat too long before a kitsune-in-disguise is taken as a vow; bow carelessly to the wrong fox and you may owe it a favor (on) you didn't intend to promise.

culturalCodex.topic: Shrine vs. temple — and how to pray at each
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: A Shintō SHRINE (jinja) is marked by a torii gate; a Buddhist TEMPLE (tera/-dera) has a larger roofed gate and often a pagoda. AT A SHRINE: bow twice, clap twice, make your wish, bow once more (ni-rei, ni-hakushu, ichi-rei). AT A TEMPLE: do NOT clap — press your palms together silently, bow, and pray. Toss a small coin (a 5-yen coin, 'go-en,' is lucky because it's a homophone for 'good fortune/relationship') into the offering box first.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The Pillar Temple of Pure Water is a TEMPLE — clap there and the carved Kannon 'wake and listen,' alerting the fox-cell to the party's presence. Clapping correctly at the thousand-torii SHRINE, by contrast, opens the inner path.

culturalCodex.topic: Temizu — purifying at the water basin
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Before approaching a shrine, stop at the temizuya (water pavilion). Take the ladle (hishaku) in your RIGHT hand, rinse your LEFT hand; switch hands, rinse the right; return to the right hand, pour a little water into your cupped left palm and rinse your mouth (don't touch the ladle to your lips); rinse the left hand again; then tip the ladle upright so the last water runs down the handle to clean it for the next person. Never drink directly from the ladle.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: The water-spirit of the thousand-torii basin reads intent in the care of the ritual. Purify sloppily and the onibi fox-fire treats you as prey; purify with grace and the first stone fox you pass dips its head a fraction in approval.

culturalCodex.topic: Omikuji — paper fortunes and tying off bad luck
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: At shrines and temples you can draw an omikuji (paper fortune), usually by shaking a numbered stick from a box or paying ~100-200 yen. Rankings run roughly from dai-kichi (great blessing) down through kichi (blessing) to kyō (curse) and dai-kyō (great curse). If you draw a BAD fortune, fold it and tie it to the designated rack of strings or a pine branch at the shrine — leaving the bad luck BEHIND you. A good fortune you may keep.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: At the halfway rest on the torii path, every single omikuji has come up dai-kyō for a month straight — an impossible run that is the rice-god's own warning. A bad fortune tied to the rack here doesn't just shed luck; it pins a thread the foxes can follow back to you.

culturalCodex.topic: Torii gates — what they are and who pays for them
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: A torii is the gateway that marks the boundary between the ordinary world and the sacred ground of a Shintō shrine; passing under one, it's polite to bow slightly and to walk to the SIDE rather than straight up the center (the center is the kami's path). At Fushimi Inari in Kyoto, thousands of vermilion torii form tunnels up the mountain — each one DONATED by a business or individual, with the donor's name and the date inscribed on the back of the gate.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: Reading the donors' names on the BACKS of the gates is a literal clue: the Akagane merchant house bought a long run of new gates all at once in fox-gold, and that suspicious stretch hides the stair down to the undershrine.

culturalCodex.topic: Foxes, Inari, and fried tofu offerings
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Inari Ōkami is the Shintō deity of rice, prosperity, and merchants; the white foxes (kitsune) at Inari shrines are the god's MESSENGERS, not gods themselves — that's why stone foxes guard these shrines, often holding a key, a jewel, a scroll, or a rice-sheaf in their mouths. The traditional food offering is abura-age (fried tofu), which folklore says foxes love — hence 'kitsune udon,' noodles topped with fried tofu.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: A real bowl of kitsune udon left at a stone fox's feet buys a moment of the spirit's goodwill; in the undershrine, knowing that the stone foxes hold key/jewel/scroll/rice tells you which statue conceals the iron key and which one's gaze points to Hōen's altar.

culturalCodex.topic: Shoes off, and the genkan step
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: Remove your shoes at the genkan (the recessed entry step) of homes, traditional inns (ryokan), tatami-floored teahouses, and the inner buildings of temples. Step UP onto the floor without letting your socked foot touch the lower stone, and turn your shoes to point back toward the door. House slippers are often provided — but NEVER wear any slippers onto tatami mats, and use the separate toilet slippers only in the toilet (then take them off again).
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: A zashiki-warashi house-spirit at the Hundred-Petal Teahouse silently judges every guest by whether they line their shoes up neatly at the genkan; tidy guests find the tea sweeter and the geiko more forthcoming.

culturalCodex.topic: Ordering at a teahouse / eating manners
culturalCodex.real: ✅ Real: In casual spots you'll often get a hot or cold hand-towel (oshibori) — wipe your hands, not your face, and set it aside. Say 'itadakimasu' before eating and 'gochisōsama (deshita)' after. Slurping noodles is normal and even polite. NEVER stick your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice or pass food chopstick-to-chopstick (both evoke funeral rites). Pour drinks for your companions rather than yourself. Tipping is not customary; at a register, place cash on the little TRAY, not in the clerk's hand. Note: a true Gion ochaya traditionally serves only by introduction ('ichigen-san okotowari'), so most visitors enjoy tea/sweets at ordinary teahouses instead.
culturalCodex.fantasy: 🐉 Fantasy: Old Kenji at the Slurping Crane noodle stall will only share the safe entry-sequence to the inner shrine with a guest who orders correctly, slurps without shame, and leaves the customary last bite for the kami of the hearth.

acts.title: Act 1: The Capital of a Thousand Rumors
acts.description: The party enters Heian-kyō, delivers (or fails to deliver) their fox-sealed offering, and learns that the capital's restlessness runs deeper than nervous gossip. This act is investigation and social play: working the canal district and the teahouse quarter, mastering the etiquette that opens doors, meeting the geiko Yumesaki who holds the other half of the offering, and surviving a first brush with the conspiracy's lesser yōkai. It establishes the central tension — not every fox is a foe, and telling friend from foe is the whole game.
objectives: Enter the city and present the letter of introduction at the Sō-ke Exchange House
Gather rumors in the Willow Canal District about the troubled shrine
Earn an introduction to the geiko Yumesaki in the Lantern Teahouse District
Learn that the offering must be joined with its other half and delivered to the inner shrine
Survive the first appearance of the rival shinobi and the fox-fire onibi

scenes.name: Petals on the Willow Water
scenes.description: The party arrives at the canal-gate of Heian-kyō as evening lanterns are lit. The bustle of the Willow Canal District is overwhelming and welcoming at once — boats, stalls, monks, willows trailing in green water. Here they get their first taste of the city's manners and its rumors, and their first sense that something has the capital on edge.
scenes.readAloud: "The torii road ends at a stone canal-gate, and Heian-kyō opens before you like a lacquered box. 🏮 Weeping willows trail their green fingers in slow water; flat-bottomed boats slide beneath a humpbacked bridge where a blind man plucks a biwa and sings the day's news for coppers. The air is charcoal-smoke and frying tofu and river-mud. A monk rattles his iron bowl; a red-bibbed stone Jizō watches the road, a little pyramid of pebbles stacked at its feet by travelers asking for safe passage. It should be a merry scene — and yet. The lanterns gutter and flare though there is no wind. A pilgrim hurries past clutching a paper fortune and muttering, and you catch the word he keeps repeating: 'dai-kyō... dai-kyō...' Great curse. Great curse."

skillChecks.success: The cheerful bustle is a brave face. Conversations die when the eastern mountain — and its thousand red gates — is mentioned. People are frightened of the shrine, the one place that should make them feel safe.
skillChecks.failure: It seems a normal, busy evening in a great city; the unease doesn't register yet.

skillChecks.success: You recall that the Great Shrine of a Thousand Torii is sacred to Inari, god of rice and fortune, whose white foxes carry prayers between worlds. A troubled Inari shrine is an ill omen for the entire capital's prosperity.
skillChecks.failure: You know it's an important shrine but not why a fox would be carrying letters around.

skillChecks.success: On a rooftop above the bridge, a figure in a slate-gray hood watches the crowd — watches YOU, specifically — then slips out of sight the instant you notice. They moved like a trained shinobi.
skillChecks.failure: The rooftops are just rooftops; you notice nothing.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the soft open. Reward etiquette: a player who bows, offers a pebble to Jizō, or uses 'sumimasen' to flag the noodle-stall owner earns warmer responses and freer rumors (flag these as ✅ Real customs as they come up). Old Kenji at the Slurping Crane noodle stall is the key NPC here — a retired shrine-warden who plays dumb but warms quickly to courteous, hungry travelers. He plants three rumors: (1) the omikuji at the shrine have all come up 'great curse' for a month; (2) pilgrims who climb the gates after dusk don't all come back; (3) 'if you want the truth of the shrine, you'll need the ear of a certain geiko in Hanagiku-machi — but you don't just walk into an ochaya; you need an introduction.' The tanuki leaf-money bit (✅ Real folklore) is a fun optional beat that earns the party a minor favor.
loot: A skewer of grilled rice-cake and a bowl of kitsune udon from Old Kenji (and his goodwill, worth more than gold)
A 5-yen 'go-en' lucky coin pressed on them by a grateful monk (narrative luck token; ✅ Real: 5-yen coins are the customary, lucky shrine offering)

scenes.name: An Introduction in the Lantern Lanes
scenes.description: Following Old Kenji's lead, the party seeks an introduction into the Lantern Teahouse District and an audience with the geiko Yumesaki at the Hundred-Petal Teahouse. This is a scene of refined social navigation — manners are the dungeon here, and a misstep closes doors that courtesy would have opened.
scenes.readAloud: "Hanagiku-machi 🏮 is another world from the canal bustle — narrow stone lanes lit entirely by rows of red lanterns, the wooden teahouses shuttered behind latticed fronts, the air perfumed with incense and the low pluck of a shamisen drifting from an upper room. A maiko hurries past on tall geta, her painted face a pale moon, and does not meet your eyes. At the lane's end glows the Hundred-Petal Teahouse, and at its threshold a recessed step — the genkan — where a row of guests' shoes sits neatly turned toward the door. A servant in indigo kneels at the entrance, regards your travel-stained party, and says, with devastating politeness: 'Sumimasen. The Hundred-Petal serves by introduction only. May I ask... who has sent you?'"

skillChecks.success: Naming Old Kenji (or the fox-letter, or both) and observing the threshold courtesies wins you a place at a private tea. The screen slides aside.
skillChecks.failure: Without a credible introduction you're turned away — gently, immutably. You'll need to return with Kenji's name, the letter, or a better approach.

skillChecks.success: If invited in, you navigate the tea ritual with grace — accepting the bowl with both hands, turning it, complimenting the season's sweet. Yumesaki is charmed and speaks more freely.
skillChecks.failure: You fumble the etiquette (slurp the tea, or worse); Yumesaki remains courteous but guarded, and reveals less.

skillChecks.success: Watching Yumesaki closely, you notice the impossible: in the candlelight her shadow on the screen has, for just a heartbeat, the silhouette of a fox with many tails — and she sees you see it. She is not your enemy. She is terrified of being SEEN.
skillChecks.failure: She is poised, beautiful, and entirely unreadable; you learn only what she chooses to tell.

scenes.roleplayNotes: CRITICAL etiquette teaching moment — surface the ✅ Real customs explicitly: shoes off and turned toward the door at the genkan; the zashiki-warashi house-spirit favors tidy guests; accepting tea with both hands; 'itadakimasu' before the sweet. Yumesaki is the heart of Act 1: she is secretly a hundred-year (eventually nine-tail) kitsune who has chosen to guard the capital. She holds the SECOND HALF of the party's offering — the two halves of a lacquered seal that, joined, prove the bearer is sanctioned by Inari herself. She explains the danger in elegant indirection: a clever young fox beneath the shrine has 'forgotten that a messenger is not a master,' the elder foxes have 'gone quiet, one by one,' and the party must reach the inner shrine to deliver the joined offering. She CANNOT openly reveal her own fox-nature without being driven from the city — play her fear of exposure as real and sympathetic. If the party is kind and discreet about what they glimpsed, she becomes their most powerful ally in Act 3.
loot: The second half of the fox-sealed offering — a lacquered half-disc that clicks magnetically against the party's box (quest item)
Yumesaki's folding fan, painted with a single white fox — show it at the shrine gate and the wardens will admit you (quest item / access token)
A small lacquered comb worth 20 gp, gifted as a courtesy if the party impressed her

scenes.name: Fox-Fire on the Rooftops
scenes.description: Leaving the teahouse, the party is intercepted — the rival shinobi who has been shadowing them moves to steal the offering before it can be joined and delivered, and the conspiracy's onibi fox-fire drifts in to herd the party off-balance. The first real combat, on rain-slick lantern-lit lanes.
scenes.readAloud: "You step back out into the red-lantern night, the joined offering warm against your chest 🏮 — and the lanterns all gutter out at once. In the sudden dark, three points of pale blue flame kindle in the air at head-height, drifting, bobbing, beautiful and wrong: onibi, fox-fire 🔥, the lure that walks pilgrims off cliffs. And down the lane, a gray-hooded figure rises from a crouch on the teahouse eaves, a short blade reversed along one forearm. 'The fox's little errand-runners,' the shinobi says softly. 'Hand me the box, and you can keep your hands.' 💀"

skillChecks.success: The onibi aren't attacking — they're LURING, drifting toward the dark mouth of an alley and the canal's edge beyond. Follow them and you'll be over the water in the dark. Hold position and they're far less dangerous.
skillChecks.failure: The drifting lights seem hypnotic and harmless; it's easy to step toward them without noticing the canal-drop ahead.

skillChecks.success: You hold your footing on the rain-slick stone and aren't drawn toward the canal edge.
skillChecks.failure: You're herded back a pace toward the dark drop to the water; next round, save vs. falling in (DC 12 Dexterity) if you don't reorient.

enemies: 1 rival shinobi (use Spy stats, AC 12, HP 27, reflavored with a short blade and smoke-step)
3 onibi fox-fire (use Will-o'-Wisp flavor on Sprite/Steam Mephit-lite stats: AC 13, HP 7 each, faint-blue fire, lure rather than slay)
combatEncounters.tactics: The shinobi opens with a thrown smoke-pellet (lightly obscured, 10 ft) and tries to cut the offering free in melee, disengaging across the rooftops if reduced below half HP — they are a recurring foe, not a corpse, and will flee to report. The onibi never close to kill; each turn they drift toward the canal edge and any creature within 5 ft that fails a DC 12 Wisdom save is compelled to step one square toward them (toward the water). Onibi wink out instantly if struck, but reappear if the party chases the lights into the dark.
combatEncounters.terrain: Narrow stone lane, rain-slick (difficult footing on a failed DC 10 check when dashing), sheer one-story drop to the canal on the east side, extinguished lanterns making the lane lightly obscured until relit. Rooftop eaves give the shinobi a high path to escape.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The lesson of this fight is the lesson of the whole module: don't take the bait. Parties that chase the pretty lights or the fleeing shinobi get split up and dunked in the canal; parties that hold formation and target the shinobi win cleanly. The shinobi is a PERSON — capturable, and a source of intelligence (they were hired in fox-gold by 'a one-tail who calls himself Hōen' and don't actually know they're working for a fox). If captured and treated decently, they can be flipped or at least bought off in Act 3. Do NOT kill the shinobi off-screen if they flee; bring them back. Award XP for the encounter however it resolves (capture, rout, or kill), and remember the onibi are worth XP too if dispersed.
loot: If the shinobi is defeated/captured: a purse of 18 gp in odd, slightly-too-warm coins (fox-gold — turns to oak leaves at the next dawn unless spent before then; ✅ Real folklore nod, 🐉 fantasy mechanic)
A coil of black silk climbing-rope and a set of three smoke-pellets (each: action to throw, 10-ft lightly obscured cloud for 1 round)
A wax-sealed contract slip naming the paymaster only as 'H., beneath the gates' — a direct clue to the undershrine

acts.title: Act 2: The Ten Thousand Gates
acts.description: Armed with the joined offering and Yumesaki's fan, the party climbs the thousand-torii path toward the inner shrine and crosses the valley to the great pillar-temple to learn the truth of the kitsune war. This act blends exploration, a festival set-piece, a yōkai ambush, and the crucial intelligence that wins or loses the finale: the words of sealing, and how to tell a benevolent fox from a malicious one. It ends with the party finding the hidden descent beneath the Akagane gates.
objectives: Purify correctly and ascend the Thousand Torii Path toward the inner shrine
Read the gate inscriptions to identify the Akagane family's suspicious donations
Survive the night festival and the kasa-obake ambush
Consult Abbot Genmyō at the Pillar Temple and learn the words of sealing
Locate the hidden descent to the Undershrine of Nine Tails

scenes.name: The Climb of Ten Thousand Gates
scenes.description: The party ascends the Senbon-Torii — the tunnel of vermilion gates climbing the mountain. Purification, etiquette, and a sharp eye for the gate inscriptions all matter here. The deeper they go, the fewer pilgrims they meet, and the more the gates seem to whisper.
scenes.readAloud: "At the foot of the mountain stands the temizuya — the purification basin, water spilling clear and cold from a bronze dragon's mouth. Beyond it, the path begins: a tunnel of vermilion torii ⛩️ set so close their crossbeams nearly kiss, climbing the mountain in an unbroken corridor of blood-warm light. Sunlight strains red-orange through ten thousand gates; the air cools and sweetens with cedar as you rise. Moss-furred stone foxes flank each landing, white bibs at their throats, a few with a fried tofu offering laid at their paws. 🦊 You are not alone on the path — and yet the higher you climb, the fewer pilgrims you pass, until at last it is only you, the red gates, and the soft, dry sound — almost like whispering — of the wind moving through ten thousand inscribed names."

skillChecks.success: You perform the temizu purification correctly — left hand, right hand, rinse the mouth, tip the ladle to clean the handle — and bow at each torii, walking to the side rather than up the kami's center. The first stone fox you pass dips its head a fraction. You feel WELCOME on the mountain.
skillChecks.failure: You rush the basin or stride up the gates' center; the path feels subtly hostile, and the onibi later will treat you as prey (disadvantage on the first save against them).

skillChecks.success: Reading the donors' names inscribed on the BACKS of the gates (✅ Real: each torii is donated, name on the reverse), you find a long, unbroken run of brand-new gates all paid for at once by a single house: the Akagane (Copper) merchants. No merchant donates a hundred gates in a single season — unless they're hiding something behind them.
skillChecks.failure: The names blur together; you note the gates are donated but miss the suspicious Akagane run (it can be found later with a returning clue).

skillChecks.success: At the forks where the tunnel splits and rejoins, you keep your bearings by the moss-and-sun, never getting turned around — important, because the foxes use the maze of gates to disorient prey.
skillChecks.failure: You lose the thread of the path at a fork and waste an hour doubling back; you arrive at the festival landing after dark, when the kasa-obake hunts.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the module's signature set-piece location — lean into the awe of the vermilion tunnel. Teach the ✅ Real customs in play: temizu sequence, bowing under torii and walking to the side, the donated gates with names on the back, fried tofu offerings to the stone foxes. The Akagane gate-run is the key Act 2 clue; if the party misses the Investigation check, Yumesaki's fan or Abbot Genmyō can point them back to it. Drifting through this scene, drop the omikuji beat: the halfway rest's fortune-rack is solid white with a month of tied-off dai-kyō (great curse) papers — an impossible, ominous run.
loot: A drawn omikuji (let a player draw: roll d6 — 1 is dai-kyō 'great curse,' 6 is dai-kichi 'great blessing'; tie a bad one to the rack to shed it, ✅ Real custom)
A small foil-wrapped Inari blessing-charm (omamori) bought at the rest stall (narrative protection; ✅ Real: omamori are amulets sold at shrines)

scenes.name: Lanterns and Paper Umbrellas — the Night Festival
scenes.description: Night falls at the halfway shrine-landing, where a small festival (matsuri) is underway — food stalls, paper lanterns, a portable shrine. But the conspiracy hides in plain sight: a possessed kasa-obake (paper-umbrella yōkai) lurks among the votive umbrellas, and a malicious one-tail fox in pilgrim's guise circulates, testing the party. The festival is a social/combat blend that rewards reading the crowd.
scenes.readAloud: "The halfway landing blazes with a little festival against the dark 🏮 — paper lanterns strung between the gates, stalls selling grilled squid and sweet shaved ice, the boom of a single drum, and a portable shrine (mikoshi) waiting to be carried up the mountain at midnight. Pilgrims laugh too loudly, as if to keep the dark at bay. Against one gate leans a rack of votive paper umbrellas left by the faithful — bright oil-paper, spinning slightly in a wind you cannot feel. And one of them, you slowly realize, has a single great rolling EYE in its center, a long red TONGUE lolling from beneath its ribs, and is hopping, on its one wooden leg, very quietly, toward the back of your smallest companion. 💀"

skillChecks.success: You spot the kasa-obake among the votive umbrellas BEFORE it pounces, and you also clock a 'pilgrim' at the squid-stall whose shadow has one too many tails — a one-tail fox scout, watching to see if you can tell its kind apart.
skillChecks.failure: The umbrella's lunge takes you by surprise (it acts first, with advantage), and the fox-scout melts into the crowd unnoticed.

skillChecks.success: The 'lost pilgrim' who asks you the way is testing you: their questions probe whether you trust foxes blindly or judge them. Answer with discernment — neither fox-hating nor fox-fawning — and the scout reports you as 'dangerous to Hōen,' which (ironically) earns you a wary respect that helps in Act 3.
skillChecks.failure: You either trust the 'pilgrim' completely (and are marked an easy mark) or insult all foxes (and harden the elders against you); either way you lose a thread of goodwill.

enemies: 1 kasa-obake possessed paper-umbrella (use Flying Sword stats reflavored: AC 14, HP 17, hops on one leg, licks with its long tongue for 1d6 + slimes a held item, vulnerable to fire but the crowd makes fire risky)
2 onibi fox-fire (AC 13, HP 7, lure as before)
combatEncounters.tactics: The kasa-obake fights cruel and comedic — it tries to lick weapons out of grips (target makes DC 12 Strength save or drops a held item, knocked 1d6 ft away) and to bowl over the smallest PC. It avoids open flame (vulnerable to fire), but using fire amid the paper-lantern festival risks a DC 12 check to avoid setting a stall alight (a complication, not a railroad). The onibi drift at the dark edges of the landing, luring stragglers toward the ravine. The one-tail fox scout does NOT join the fight — it watches, judging, and leaves.
combatEncounters.terrain: Crowded festival landing strung with flammable paper lanterns and umbrellas; a portable shrine that must not be damaged (harming the mikoshi turns the crowd against the party); a sheer ravine-drop on the downhill side where the onibi lure.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Tonally this is the module's 'spooky-fun' high point — a yōkai fight at a night festival, full of ⛩️🏮💀 flavor. The kasa-obake is more nuisance than killer; play it for comedy and tension, not lethality. The real content is the fox-scout's TEST (Insight DC 13): the module's thesis is that foxes are neither all-good nor all-evil, and the party's stance here echoes into the finale. Reward discernment, punish both blind trust and blanket fox-hatred. After the fight, a grateful festival-keeper can confirm the Akagane gate-run rumor and point the party across the valley to Abbot Genmyō at the Pillar Temple for 'the words that bind a fox without breaking it.'
loot: The kasa-obake's oil-paper canopy, salvageable as a fine waxed-paper umbrella (waterproof, 5 gp; oddly always points downhill)
Festival winnings if the party plays a stall game: a goldfish in a bag, a sack of sweet rice-dumplings (dango, 6 on the skewer — track them!), and 3 gp in change
A festival-keeper's gift: a paper lantern that relights itself once per night (narrative light source)

scenes.name: The Pillar Temple and the Words of Sealing
scenes.description: Crossing the valley to the great pillar-temple (the analog of Kiyomizu-dera), the party consults the abbot Genmyō, learns the full shape of the kitsune conspiracy, and earns the ritual words needed to resolve it without indiscriminate slaughter. A scene of revelation, reverence, and one sharply-taught etiquette distinction: this is a TEMPLE, not a shrine.
scenes.readAloud: "Across the valley, the Pillar Temple of Pure Water 🛕 thrusts its great worship-hall out over the steep hillside on a forest of tall wooden pillars, joined — the monks will proudly tell you — without a single nail. From its terrace the whole capital glitters below, lantern by lantern. At the cliff's foot, a sacred spring splits into three slender channels, each caught by pilgrims in long-handled ladles. A roofed gate and a vermilion pagoda mark this clearly as a Buddhist temple, not a Shintō shrine. An old monk in faded saffron waits for you on the terrace as though he has known you were coming. 'You carry a fox's seal,' says Abbot Genmyō, without turning. 'And the fox beneath the gates has begun to eat his elders. Press your palms together, travelers — and do NOT clap. Not here.' 💀"

skillChecks.success: You honor the temple correctly — palms pressed silently, a coin in the box, a bow, NO clap (clapping is for Shintō shrines, not Buddhist temples). Genmyō's wary courtesy warms to genuine help.
skillChecks.failure: Someone claps out of habit — and the carved Kannon in the hall behind you seem to TURN their painted eyes. Genmyō goes pale: 'You have told the foxes we spoke. Be quick now.' (Narrative cost: Hōen is forewarned, granting his thralls a small initiative edge in the finale.)

skillChecks.success: Genmyō judges you discerning enough to be trusted with the kotodama — the words of sealing — a chant that binds a MALICIOUS fox harmlessly into stone while leaving a benevolent one untouched. (Mechanically: in the finale, a character who speaks the words as an action forces a true malicious fox to make a Wisdom save or be restrained, then petrified; it has no effect on a good-hearted fox.)
skillChecks.failure: He shares the conspiracy's shape but withholds the binding words until the party proves their discernment (e.g., by freeing the charmed novice monk below).

skillChecks.success: You notice a young novice monk hovering at the hall's edge whose eyes are glassy and whose answers are a beat too smooth — he is charmed, feeding the foxes the temple's secrets. He can be gently freed (a kind word and the temple's pure water break the charm), which earns Genmyō's full trust.
skillChecks.failure: The novice seems merely shy; his betrayal goes unnoticed until it costs you.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The pivotal exposition + reward scene. Teach the ✅ Real temple-vs-shrine distinction hard here, because it pays off mechanically (no clapping at a temple; clap only at the shrine). Surface the ✅ Real Otowa three-stream custom: a character may drink from ONE of the three spring channels (the center grants the finale blessing — advantage on the first save vs. fox illusion); a greedy character who drinks from more than one forfeits all (✅ Real etiquette, 🐉 fantasy mechanic). Genmyō lays out the truth plainly: Hōen, a clever ONE-tail fox, has been devouring his elders' spirits to climb toward nine tails and godhood, sealing the benevolent elders into stone to silence them. The party's tools for the finale are (1) the joined offering + Yumesaki's fan to gain entry, (2) the kotodama words of sealing, (3) the Tail-Counting Mirror in the undershrine, and (4) discernment. Freeing the charmed novice is a clean way for a party that failed the Persuasion check to still earn the words. End by confirming the descent lies behind the Akagane gates.
loot: The kotodama — the words of sealing (quest ability; binds a malicious fox, harmless to a good one)
If a character honored the one-stream custom: the Pure Water blessing (advantage on their first save vs. fox illusion in Act 3)
A blessed prayer-bead bracelet (juzu) from Genmyō (narrative ward against charm; ✅ Real: juzu are Buddhist prayer beads)
A hand-copied map marking the gap behind the Akagane gates where the undershrine stair descends

acts.title: Act 3: The Counting of Tails
acts.description: The party descends behind the Akagane gates into the drowned Undershrine of Nine Tails, confronts Hōen the schemer, and must resolve the crisis with discernment rather than slaughter — telling trapped allies from stone decoys, freeing the elder spirits Hōen stole, and exposing how few tails he truly has. Yumesaki may reveal her true nature; the rival shinobi may turn. The act rewards everything the party learned about etiquette, mercy, and reading a fox.
objectives: Descend behind the Akagane gates into the Undershrine of Nine Tails
Use the Tail-Counting Mirror to tell true allies from Hōen's decoys
Free the petrified elder foxes Hōen has silenced
Confront Hōen and seal or break him without slaughtering the innocent
Deliver the offering, restore the shrine, and decide the foxes' fate

scenes.name: Descent Behind the Copper Gates
scenes.description: The party finds the gap behind the Akagane family's suspicious gate-run and descends into the undershrine — a drowned, fox-fire-lit vermilion ruin full of stone foxes, some of which are not stone at all. A scene of dread, discovery, and the first hard choice: which stone foxes are weeping?
scenes.readAloud: "Behind the newest, reddest gates — the ones the Akagane house paid for in too much gold — a single torii stands crooked, and behind it the mountain simply... opens. Stone steps descend into cold cedar-dark, lit only by the slow drift of pale-blue onibi 🔥. The air smells of wet stone and old incense. The stair lets out into a sunken shrine drowned in cedar-root, its vermilion faded to the color of old blood 💀, and everywhere — EVERYWHERE — sit stone foxes 🦊, hundreds of them, ranked in the dark, their carved eyes catching the fox-fire. And as you stand there, you hear it, very faint, from somewhere in that field of statues: the sound of weeping. Stone does not weep. Some of these foxes are not stone at all."

skillChecks.success: Among the hundreds of statues, you pick out the ones that are subtly WRONG — a tear-track of real moisture, a chest that rises a hair's breadth, warmth where stone should be cold. These are the petrified elder foxes, alive inside the stone, and there are seven of them.
skillChecks.failure: The statues all look the same in the fox-fire; you can't yet tell the prisoners from the props (you'll need the Mirror or an elder's help).

skillChecks.success: You find which stone fox holds a KEY in its mouth (a real iron key hidden in a hollow behind it, opening the altar-rail) and which holds a SCROLL (its carved gaze points dead-straight at the black-lacquer altar where Hōen waits). The old fox-statue lore pays off.
skillChecks.failure: You note the foxes hold keys, jewels, scrolls, and rice-sheaves, but not which one matters.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Dread and discovery, no combat yet — let the horror of the weeping statues land. This scene sets up the finale's central skill: telling true from false. The seven petrified elders are the party's potential allies; freeing even some of them before the boss fight dramatically eases it. The ✅ Real fox-statue lore (key/jewel/scroll/rice-sheaf in the mouth) becomes a literal navigation tool here — reward players who remember it from the codex. If Yumesaki accompanied the party (earned in Act 1), this is where she can quietly confirm which statues weep, at the cost of revealing more of her nature.
loot: An iron altar-key hidden behind the key-holding fox statue (opens the rail around Hōen's altar and the elders' restraints)
A censer of sweet incense from a side-niche (lighting it grants the party advantage on saves vs. fox-fear for 10 minutes)

scenes.name: The Tail-Counting Mirror
scenes.description: At the heart of the undershrine the party finds the bronze Tail-Counting Mirror, which shows a fox's true number of tails to anyone who looks while speaking truth. Used well, it lets the party free the right prisoners and unmask Hōen's central lie before the fight — or expose a 'helpful' ally as a fraud, or confirm a suspected friend.
scenes.readAloud: "Past the ranks of stone foxes, a bronze mirror hangs on a frame of black lacquer, its surface dark and rippling like still water. Above it, carved characters read: 'Look, and speak true, and see how many tails.' 🦊 Beside the mirror, a black-lacquer altar bears a censer notched nine times — and eight of the nine notches glow with a stolen, captive light. One notch remains empty. Whatever is being counted here, it is nearly complete."

skillChecks.success: You understand the Mirror: it shows truth only to one who speaks truth before it. Hold up a stone-fox prisoner before it and speak honestly, and the glass reveals the living elder within and how to break the petrification (the iron key + the kotodama spoken kindly). Hold up Yumesaki (if present) and she shows as a NINE-tail — proof beyond doubt that she is an ancient guardian, not a foe.
skillChecks.failure: The mirror stays dark and rippling; it will not answer until someone speaks a true thing before it.

skillChecks.success: The censer's eight stolen lights and one empty notch tell the story: Hōen has devoured EIGHT elder spirits and needs only ONE more to claim a ninth tail and godhood. He is, right now, a fox with stolen power and only ONE true tail of his own — theft, not strength. Strip the stolen spirits and he is nothing.
skillChecks.failure: The censer is clearly significant and clearly almost full, but its exact meaning is unclear.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The Mirror is the module's truth-engine and the GM's tool for paying off Act 1's central mystery: it lets a suspicious party finally confirm that Yumesaki is an ally (nine tails) and that Hōen is a fraud (one tail). It also reveals the method to free the petrified elders: the iron altar-key + the kotodama words spoken with compassion (NOT the malicious-binding usage) restores a good fox to flesh. Encourage the party to free as many of the seven elders as they can BEFORE confronting Hōen — each freed elder is an ally in the boss fight and a stolen spirit Hōen can't keep. This is the lever that turns a deadly fight into a winnable one. Do NOT let the Mirror lie or hedge — honor its truth absolutely, in keeping with the dice-and-stat integrity rules.
loot: Knowledge: the method to free the petrified elders (iron key + kotodama spoken with kindness)
Knowledge: Hōen has one true tail; his stolen lights can be released back to their stone bodies

scenes.name: Hōen, and How Many Tails the Moon Has
scenes.description: The climactic confrontation with Hōen the one-tail schemer at the black-lacquer altar. The fight is winnable by force but DESIGNED to be won by discernment: free the elders, expose his single tail, seal or simply break his confidence. The offering is delivered, the ninth notch denied, and the foxes' fate decided.
scenes.readAloud: "At the black altar, a slender young man in vermilion robes turns to greet you, and his smile is beautiful and starving. Behind him, the censer's eight stolen lights pulse hungrily toward the ninth empty notch. 'You're the courier,' Hōen says, delighted. 'And you brought the offering right to me. How thoughtful.' His shadow on the drowned wall spreads into NINE proud tails — but the Tail-Counting Mirror beside you shows the truth: a single, ordinary, frightened tail. 🦊💀 'Kneel,' he purrs, 'and I'll let your little capital keep its rice. Refuse, and I take your spirits for my ninth.' One notch left. The whole city's fortune balanced on it. Roll initiative — or don't. The choice, as it has been all along, is whether you can tell what's truly in front of you."

skillChecks.success: Speaking the kotodama words of sealing as an action forces Hōen (a true malicious fox) to make a DC 13 Wisdom save or be restrained, then petrified on a second failure — the same fate he inflicted on his elders. Poetic, and decisive.
skillChecks.failure: Your pronunciation falters; the binding fails this round, but you may try again (Hōen gains a free action to lash out).

skillChecks.success: Holding the Mirror to his face and naming his ONE true tail aloud shatters his illusion of nine; his charmed thralls, seeing him small, waver and may break free (DC drops for freeing them).
skillChecks.failure: He laughs off the accusation for now; the thralls hold.

skillChecks.success: If even three elders have been freed, you can rally them and the wavering thralls to surround Hōen without bloodshed — he surrenders rather than be torn apart by the very elders he wronged.
skillChecks.failure: Words alone won't end it; it comes down to the seal or the sword.

enemies: Hōen, the one-tail schemer (use Cult Fanatic stats reflavored: AC 13, HP 33, charm and illusion magic, fox-fire bolt 1d10; loses HP and spell access as stolen spirits are freed)
2 charmed shinobi or thralls (Spy/Bandit stats, AC 12, HP 27/11; can be freed from the charm, not just killed)
combatEncounters.tactics: Hōen opens with illusion (the nine-tail shadow; a DC 13 Wisdom save to disbelieve, with advantage to anyone who took the Pure Water blessing) and tries to charm the party's strongest fighter. KEY DESIGN: each petrified elder the party freed BEFORE this fight removes one of Hōen's stolen lights — reduce his HP by 5 and remove one spell/round per freed elder, and a freed elder fights at the party's side. Freeing elders MID-fight (iron key + kotodama spoken kindly, an action) weakens him in real time. The charmed thralls can be freed (DC 12 with the temple's pure water, a kind word, or breaking line of sight to Hōen) rather than slain. If the party speaks the sealing kotodama successfully, Hōen is bound regardless of HP. Honor the dice and the stats — if the party simply brawls without freeing elders, this is a genuinely hard, possibly lethal fight, exactly as written; no phantom rescues.
combatEncounters.terrain: Drowned vermilion shrine, ankle-deep cold runoff (difficult terrain in the low center), ranks of stone foxes for cover (and for freeing), the black-lacquer altar with its nine-notch censer, drifting onibi at the edges. The Tail-Counting Mirror stands beside the altar and can be picked up and used as an action.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The emotional and mechanical climax. Hōen is a tragedy of ambition, not a cackling devil — a clever, frightened young fox who decided godhood was worth eating his elders. He can be SEALED (poetic justice, petrified as he petrified others), BROKEN (stripped of stolen spirits, he collapses into an ordinary, weeping fox who can be shown mercy or exile), or KILLED (valid, but the elders will mourn that it came to that). The intended 'best' outcome is to free the elders and break/seal him without a bloodbath — but honor whatever the party earns. Yumesaki, if she came, reveals her nine tails openly here and helps turn the tide; the rival shinobi, if captured and treated decently in Act 1, can switch sides upon learning they were duped by 'fox-gold.' Once Hōen is dealt with and the censer's stolen lights released back to their stone bodies, ALL seven elders return to flesh. The party finally OPENS the offering before the altar (as instructed) — inside is the missing ninth spirit, the eldest fox of all, whom Hōen could never catch, returned to crown the restored shrine. Award full XP for the encounter (Hōen + thralls + onibi), plus a generous milestone for resolving it with discernment.
loot: The black-lacquer altar's offerings: 120 gp in genuine (non-fox) shrine-gold, split as the party sees fit
The Tail-Counting Mirror (minor wondrous item: once per day, reflect a creature to learn if it is shapechanged/illusory and its true form)
Hōen's vermilion robe, woven with real silver thread (40 gp), and his single fox-tail brush (a calligraphy brush of fine make, 15 gp)
A grateful elder fox's gift: a kitsune charm (omamori) granting advantage on the FIRST save against any charm or illusion, once, then it crumbles to oak leaves

scenes.name: Two Bows, Two Claps, One Bow
scenes.description: The denouement. The shrine restored, the elders freed, and Hōen dealt with, the party at last completes the delivery and the proper rite at the inner shrine — and decides, with the foxes, what the capital's relationship to its kami will be going forward. Yumesaki, the offering, and the party's accumulated choices all come due.
scenes.readAloud: "Dawn finds you back at the inner shrine, the thousand torii above you no longer whispering but simply, peacefully red in the morning light. ⛩️ The seven elder foxes — flesh again, fur silver with age — sit in a quiet ring, and among them, no longer hiding, stands Yumesaki, nine tails fanned behind her like a sunrise. The offering box rests open on the altar; the eldest spirit has come home. There is one thing left to do, and you know it now: you step to the offering box, and you bow twice, and you clap twice, and you bow once more — the rite of a Shintō shrine, done right at last. The bell rings of its own accord. Somewhere far below in the capital, ten thousand guttering lanterns steady and burn clean and bright. 🦊🏮 'The vigil is kept,' says the eldest fox, in a voice like rice rustling in the wind. 'And the gates remember their friends. What would you ask of Inari's foxes, traveler?'"

skillChecks.success: You complete the shrine rite flawlessly — bow twice, clap twice, pray, bow once (✅ Real) — and the offering is accepted with full honor; the capital's fortune is restored and the party is named friends of the shrine.
skillChecks.failure: You stumble the rite (or clap when you should bow, or bow when you should clap); the foxes gently correct you with great patience, and it still resolves — but the lesson lands.

skillChecks.success: You broker the foxes' future role — whether they return to quiet messenger-work, take Yumesaki as their open guardian, or extend a standing welcome to the party. The eldest grants your reasonable request, opening hooks for future scenarios across Hinomoto.
skillChecks.failure: The foxes choose their own path without the party's input, but bear them no ill will.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Pure denouement and reward — let the players decide the shape of the ending. The mechanical payoff of the whole module's etiquette teaching is this final correct shrine-rite (bow twice / clap twice / bow once), the mirror-image of the temple's NO-clap rule from Act 2 — a satisfying ✅ Real bookend. Yumesaki's open friendship, the elders' gratitude, and any flipped shinobi all become standing allies for the wider 'Floating World' campaign. If the party showed mercy to a broken (rather than sealed or killed) Hōen, the eldest fox notes it approvingly — mercy, like discernment, is the campaign's quiet virtue. Close on a hook: the eldest fox warns that 'the gates of Heian-kyō are calm, but to the east, in the Deer Park of Kasuga, the sacred deer have stopped bowing' — pointing toward the next scenario.
loot: A shrine-blessed omamori for each party member (✅ Real amulet; narrative ward, choose: traffic-safety, success-in-studies, or good-relationships — a fun real-Japan detail)
Standing rank as 'Friends of the Thousand Torii' — free lodging and a sympathetic ear at any Inari shrine in Hinomoto
If the party brokered it: a kitsune messenger who will carry one message anywhere in the land, once, on the party's behalf (campaign-level favor)

npcsInvolved.name: Yumesaki
npcsInvolved.description: A geiko (geisha) of the Hundred-Petal Teahouse, poised and luminous, her white-painted face unreadable and her every gesture a study in refinement. In truth she is an ancient kitsune — a hundred-year fox grown to nine tails — who long ago chose to love and guard the human capital rather than prey upon it. She hides her nature out of real and well-founded fear: a fox unmasked in Heian-kyō is driven out, or worse.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Yumesaki wants the capital protected and the offering delivered to restore the shrine, but she cannot act openly without revealing herself. She is testing the party throughout Act 1 — are they discerning enough to tell a good fox from a bad one? If they treat her glimpsed nature with discretion and kindness, she becomes their decisive ally in the finale. If they react with fox-hatred, she withdraws and lets them face Hōen alone.

npcsInvolved.name: Hōen, the One-Tail Schemer
npcsInvolved.description: A slender young fox in vermilion court-robes, beautiful and starving, with a smile that never quite reaches his eyes. He has only ONE true tail, but cloaks himself in the illusion of nine. Clever beyond his years and bitter at the slow, humble lot of a messenger-fox, he decided that godhood was worth devouring his own elders for.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Hōen wants to ascend to nine tails — the mark of a fox-god — by consuming the spirits of his elders, of whom he has taken eight, sealing their bodies into stone to silence them. He needs only ONE more spirit and has lured the party's offering (which contains the ninth, eldest spirit he could never catch) right to his altar. His power is theft and illusion, not true strength; strip away the stolen spirits and he is an ordinary, frightened fox. He is a villain, but a pitiable one, and the module supports sealing, breaking, or sparing him.

npcsInvolved.name: Old Kenji of the Slurping Crane
npcsInvolved.description: The grizzled, perpetually-steaming proprietor of a canal-side noodle stall, with forearms like ham-hocks and a memory like a ledger. He plays the simple noodle-cook but is in fact a retired warden of the thousand-torii shrine, who knows the safe sequence to enter the inner sanctum and the etiquette that the foxes respect.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Kenji wants the shrine — his life's old charge — set right, but he's cautious and won't help fools or the rude. He measures travelers by how they treat his food and his stall: order correctly, slurp without shame, leave the customary last bite for the hearth-kami, and he opens up. He's the party's gateway to the teahouse district and a steady source of true rumor and real etiquette.

npcsInvolved.name: The Gray Shinobi (Kageno)
npcsInvolved.description: A trained shinobi in a slate-gray hood, fast and economical, who shadows the party from the rooftops and tries to steal the offering. Hired in fox-gold by a paymaster known only as 'H., beneath the gates,' Kageno does not actually know they're working for a fox — and would not be pleased to learn the coin turns to oak leaves at dawn.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Kageno is a professional taking a contract, not a true believer. They want the offering and their fee, in that order. If captured and treated with decency rather than executed, and shown the fox-gold for the fraud it is, Kageno can be flipped or bought into switching sides for the finale — a recurring foe who becomes a reluctant ally, rewarding parties that fight with restraint.

npcsInvolved.name: Abbot Genmyō
npcsInvolved.description: The ancient abbot of the Pillar Temple of Pure Water, in faded saffron robes, calm as still water and twice as deep. He has watched the kitsune politics of the mountain for sixty years and grieves the war among the foxes — for Inari's messengers were never meant to turn on one another.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Genmyō wants the conspiracy ended without indiscriminate slaughter of foxes, most of whom are innocent or victims. He guards the kotodama — the words of sealing — and grants them only to travelers discerning enough to use them justly (binding the malicious, sparing the good). He teaches the temple-vs-shrine etiquette and the three-stream custom, and freeing his charmed novice earns his complete trust.

rewards.gold: approximately 175 gp total (18 gp fox-gold from the shinobi if spent before dawn, festival winnings, the comb/charm sales, and 120 gp of genuine shrine-gold from Hōen's altar)
items: The Tail-Counting Mirror (minor wondrous item: once/day, reflect a creature to reveal if it is shapechanged or illusory, and its true form)
A kitsune omamori charm (advantage on the first save vs. charm or illusion, once, then crumbles to oak leaves)
Yumesaki's white-fox folding fan (shrine access token / keepsake)
Abbot Genmyō's juzu prayer-bead bracelet (narrative ward against charm)
A self-relighting paper festival lantern (narrative light source)
Shrine-blessed omamori for each party member (choose: traffic-safety, success-in-studies, or good-relationships — ✅ Real amulet flavor)
Standing rank as 'Friends of the Thousand Torii' (free lodging at any Inari shrine in Hinomoto)
rewards.story: The party has unraveled a conspiracy of fox-spirits beneath the imperial capital, told true foxes from false, and restored the Great Shrine of a Thousand Torii — denying a frightened, clever fox his stolen godhood without a needless bloodbath. Their discernment and mercy have won them an ancient nine-tail guardian's friendship, the gratitude of seven freed elder foxes, and possibly a reformed shinobi at their side. Heian-kyō's lanterns burn clean again, and the party stands named friends of the shrine across all of Hinomoto. But the eldest fox's parting warning points east: in the sacred Deer Park of Kasuga, the deer have stopped bowing — and the road of ten thousand gates was only the first of the campaign's mysteries.

twists: Not all the foxes are foes — and not all are friends. The central challenge is DISCERNMENT: the geiko Yumesaki is a benevolent nine-tail guardian hiding in plain sight, while the 'helpful' young fox at the festival is a malicious scout. Players conditioned to either trust or hate all foxes will misread the entire scenario.

The villain Hōen, who cloaks himself in the illusion of NINE proud tails, in truth has only ONE. His power is theft and illusion, not strength; the Tail-Counting Mirror exposes the lie, and stripping away the spirits he stole leaves him an ordinary, frightened fox.

Hundreds of stone fox-statues fill the undershrine — and seven of them are living elder foxes petrified alive, weeping inside the stone. Freeing them BEFORE the boss fight is the lever that turns a deadly confrontation into a winnable one; each freed elder is both an ally and a stolen spirit Hōen loses.

The fox-sealed offering the party has carried since the very first scene contains the missing NINTH spirit — the eldest fox of all, the one Hōen could never catch. By delivering it to the altar (and never opening it before then, as instructed), the party unwittingly carries the conspiracy's solution in their own hands the whole journey.

The etiquette is real and load-bearing: clapping is correct at a Shintō SHRINE (the finale rite) but FORBIDDEN at a Buddhist TEMPLE (Abbot Genmyō's hall) — and getting it backwards has narrative consequences. The module's ✅ Real cultural lessons are not flavor; they are gameplay.
dmTips: Run the etiquette as the real puzzle. Don't make players guess blindly — the culturalCodex entries are written to be surfaced in play. When a character bows under a torii, washes at the temizu basin, or presses palms (without clapping) at the temple, narrate the correct ✅ Real custom and reward it. The finale's shrine-rite (bow twice, clap twice, bow once) should feel earned by everything taught earlier.

Hold the line on discernment. The module lives or dies on the players learning that foxes are neither all-good nor all-evil. Resist the urge to telegraph which fox is which; let the Insight/Perception checks and the Tail-Counting Mirror do that work. A party that blanket-distrusts foxes should genuinely lose Yumesaki's aid and face a harder finale.

Make freeing the elders matter mechanically. The Hōen fight is written as HARD on purpose. The intended path to victory is freeing the seven petrified elders (each reduces Hōen's HP by 5 and removes a spell/round, and fights at the party's side). A party that ignores this and brawls should find the fight genuinely dangerous — honor the stats, no phantom HP, no last-second rescues.

Honor the dice and the pre-declared DCs absolutely. Every skill check here lists its DC; decide nothing after the roll. The onibi lures, the kasa-obake's item-licking, the kotodama binding — all have real failure states. A failed temple-clap really does forewarn Hōen; a botched temizu really does give the onibi an edge. The integrity of the consequences is what makes the etiquette feel real.

Let mercy be an option, not a mandate. Hōen can be sealed (petrified, as he petrified others), broken (stripped and spared), or killed — all valid. The rival shinobi can be flipped or fought. Reward parties that find the non-lethal path with the elders' and Yumesaki's deeper gratitude, but never punish a party that fairly chooses the sword.

Use the ✅/🐉 tags out loud. This campaign doubles as trip-prep for a real Kyoto journey. When a real custom comes up, it's genuinely fun to say so — 'that's a real thing you can do at Fushimi Inari today' — and then layer the 🐉 fantasy twist on top. The culturalCodex gives you eight ready-made, trip-accurate beats; weave them in naturally rather than lecturing.
